extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, fiction writers, writing students and teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writers to learn craft by closely reading exemplary fiction; focuses on sentence-, paragraph-, and narrative-level techniques and how to adopt them in one’s own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close Reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Slow down; pay attention; the surface of the prose is everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best teacher of writing is close reading of great writing. Read slowly and intensively to learn craft choices; re-read passages and study how specific language, sentence shape, and detail produce effect. 'Read closely, then read more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Words
rubrics_metrics.description: The raw material of literature; precision matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose exact, appropriate words—the writer’s primary material. Study how canonical authors pick single words that carry weight and nuance; prefer precision over vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: "The well-made sentence transcends time and genre."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence-level craft is essential: syntax, rhythm, and diction shape meaning and tone. 'Sentence quality matters at the line level'—lazy sentences produce lazy stories. Study sentence construction and revise at the line level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraphs organize ideas and pacing; their length and structure control emphasis and flow. Treat paragraphs as compositional units that guide the reader’s attention and set narrative rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point of view, narrative distance, and tense are deliberate choices that determine what is revealed and how. Consider whose perception frames the story and what knowledge is withheld or granted; narration choices carry ethical weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Action, dialogue, physical description as characterization tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character should be shown through what a person does, says, and how they are described physically; avoid relying on labels or exposition. Use behavior, speech, and detail to make characters concrete and distinctive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't 'clean up' speech; capture its rhythm; learn from Le Carré on advancing plot via talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let dialogue reflect real speech patterns (without transcribing every filler). Dialogue can reveal character through diction, rhythm, and evasion and can advance plot—study writers like John le Carré for technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Details
rubrics_metrics.description: One or two telling details > paragraph of description (Flannery O'Connor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few precise, telling details are more effective than long descriptive passages. Favor small, specific images that do the work of characterization and scene-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Character actions reveal character; not 'physical clichés' but illuminations (Joyce, Mansfield).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gestures—brief physical actions—to illuminate interior life and relationships. Avoid stock or cliché movements; prefer gestures that reveal psychology or subtext.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning from Chekhov
rubrics_metrics.description: The master of restraint, compassion, ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study Chekhov for economical art: restraint in exposition, compassion for characters, and comfort with ambiguity. Emulate his balance of observation and restraint when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading for Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: The encounter with great work emboldens you to try difficult things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close reading of challenging, exemplary work gives writers the confidence to attempt bold structural, stylistic, or ethical choices in their own writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence quality matters (explicit criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence quality matters at the line level — lazy sentences = lazy story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and revise at the sentence level; strong sentences accumulate to a strong story. Watch for laziness in cadence, diction, and syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling detail beats description (explicit criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: One or two telling details are better than a paragraph of description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize specific, emblematic details that carry associative and emotional weight over extended, generalized description. Study Flannery O'Connor and Tolstoy for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture is an underused tool (explicit criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gesture is one of fiction's most underused tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively employ gesture to reveal character and subtext; use examples from Joyce and Mansfield to see how small movements convey interiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue reveals character (explicit criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue reveals character through diction, rhythm, evasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dialogue for how it shows character (word choice, pauses, what is avoided). Do not 'clean up' speech—retain rhythm and indirectness when it serves characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: POV as an ethical choice (explicit criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: POV is always a deliberate ethical choice — what is being seen, by whom, with what knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a point of view, consider the moral implications of what the narrator/ focalizer reveals or conceals. The choice of vantage point shapes sympathy, judgment, and reader understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read closely, then read more (explicit criterion)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make close reading a habitual practice: examine craft choices in many authors and accumulate examples rather than relying on abstract rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mantra: Learn from examples, not rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are no general rules; there are only specific examples."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of memorizing universal rules, study concrete examples from great writers to see how techniques function in context. Use those examples as models for practice and imitation.
